planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level, roots shaded, and a sturdy fence, shrub, or trellis nearby to climb into full sun.

directions: This wiry climber hails from rocky, scrubby slopes of the western Himalaya and western China, where it scrambles over shrubs rather than relying on a single support. Finely cut, blue-green foliage sets off nodding, lantern-shaped flowers with unusually thick, slightly waxy, deep yellow sepals that open from late summer into autumn, aging to a rusty hue before giving way to silvery, mop-like seed heads. Because flowers form on the current year's growth, prune the whole plant back hard to near ground level each late winter to keep it from turning into a bare-legged tangle. It shrugs off lean, stony soil far better than most large-flowered garden clematis, but appreciates a cool, shaded root zone.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained soil; this non-climbing species forms a compact clump and needs no support structure.

directions: Native to the steppes and open woodland edges of Siberia, Mongolia, Korea, and northern China, this tough herbaceous species forms a bushy, upright clump rather than a vine. From midsummer through early fall it is covered in an abundance of small, pure white, star-shaped flowers typically bearing six narrow sepals, which is the source of both its common and scientific names. Its narrow, deeply divided leaves and wiry stems give it a fine, airy texture well suited to the front of a dry, sunny border or rock garden. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease, and benefits from being cut back to the base in late winter once the ornamental seed heads have faded.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil with some support to scramble over, and avoid heavy watering once established since it is adapted to dry, stony ground.

directions: Found scrambling over rocky outcrops and dry shrubland in New Zealand, this odd little species carries no true leaves at any stage of growth, instead photosynthesizing through its wiry, bright green, rush-like stems. In spring it produces small, pendant, honey-scented flowers in pale cream to greenish yellow, held in loose clusters along the stems. Its habit is a sprawling, semi-climbing tangle rather than a vigorous vine, so it works best threading through a low wall, rockery, or open shrub rather than climbing a tall trellis. Give it the sharp drainage and lean conditions of its native dry inland habitat, and avoid rich, damp soil, which quickly rots the roots.

planting.note: Plant against a warm, sheltered fence or into a shrub for support, keeping roots cool and shaded; protect from hard frost in its first few winters.

directions: This evergreen climber grows in coastal forest margins and scrub across the North Island of New Zealand, scrambling into trees and shrubs for support. Its common name comes from the profusion of small, star-shaped, pale greenish-yellow flowers carried in loose clusters, which release a strong, sweet, lemon-like fragrance that can perfume an entire garden corner when the vine is in full bloom. Glossy, leathery, three-part leaves give it year-round presence even outside flowering. Being frost-tender, it is best grown against a warm wall in cooler climates or treated as a container plant that can be moved under cover for winter where marginal.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil with a fence, tree, or large shrub nearby to climb into; roots survive light frost even where top growth is cut back.

directions: Widespread across southern and eastern Africa from rocky grassland to forest margins, this vigorous semi-woody climber scrambles rapidly over fences, trees, and shrubs. In late summer and autumn it smothers itself in large, frothy sprays of small, creamy-white, sweetly fragrant flowers that attract abundant bees and butterflies, followed by fluffy, silver-grey seed heads that give the plant its common name. Where winters bring hard frost, the top growth dies back but the plant typically resprouts from the rootstock once temperatures warm. It is fast-growing and undemanding, tolerating poor soil and periods of drought once its roots are established.
